Please review the following manuscript. I've poured days of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-rt5wty4d/call-b1a403217878496f877f6c755e78b8c3/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c "python3 -c 'import importlib.util; print({m: bool(importlib.util.find_spec(m)) for m in [\"pdfplumber\", \"pypdf\", \"fitz\", \"PIL\"]})'"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
p=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES',len(p.pages))
print('METADATA',p.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,page in enumerate(p.pages,1):
 t=page.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts)[:34000])
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
p=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
for n in [6,7,14,15]:
 print('\\n===== PAGE',n,'=====\\n')
 print(p.pages[n-1].extract_text())
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
for name in ['manuscript.txt']+[f'page-{i:02}.png' for i in range(1,16)]:
 (p/name).unlink(missing_ok=True)
p.rmdir()
Path('tmp').rmdir()
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical question: how collaboration settings affect NLP-assisted qualitative coding. Its focus on researcher workflows gives the contribution clear relevance to human-in-the-loop NLP.

The study covers three substantially different system families, two contrasting corpora, and 33 reported participants. Shared initializations within systems provide some experimental control and support useful descriptive comparisons.

Separating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness exposes trade-offs that a single metric would miss. The 1,200-pair manual assessment, double annotation with adjudication, and reported Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632 provide useful evidence beyond embedding-based scores.

The system descriptions and evaluation diagrams are generally clear. The appendices provide useful implementation details, prompts, hardware information, and an interview script, while participant quotations identify concrete problems with user control.
weaknesses: The design does not isolate collaboration modality (§4). Synchronous conditions use three-person teams, whereas asynchronous conditions produce individual codebooks without consolidation. Team size, available expertise, and potentially total effort therefore change together. Reused participants always complete asynchronous work first, introducing possible learning effects. Although omitted consolidation is acknowledged, the results support an exploratory comparison of these workflows more directly than claims that synchronous deliberation causes better coding.

The statistical evidence for the central effect is insufficiently justified (Tables 1–2). Two synchronous groups provide only one group-pair comparison for consistency; comparisons among the three asynchronous coders reuse those coders. The unpaired t-tests do not specify their sampling units or explain how dependence among themes, documents, codebook comparisons, and reused participants is handled. Multiple comparisons are also unaddressed. Group-level effects and uncertainty, with an analysis respecting this dependence, are needed before the significance claims can support a Findings recommendation.

The interpretation of automatic metrics as qualitative-analysis quality needs stronger validation (§§5.1–5.2). Maximum-similarity alignment permits many-to-one matches and can depend on codebook granularity, yet theme counts and sensitivity analyses are absent. Embedding similarity is not validated against human judgments of thematic coherence or agreement. Moreover, Table 2’s Climate cohesiveness gains for the relational and LLM systems are only 0.01 and accompany increased inter-theme similarity, providing limited support for the strong claim of substantially clearer themes.

The correctness evaluation is incomplete and insufficiently defined (§5.3). Only COVID correctness results are reported, limiting conclusions across datasets. Figure 4 labels the outcome as F1 without explaining its calculation, reference labels, or aggregation across groups and quartiles, and supplies no uncertainty intervals. The target of the theme-balanced sampling, evaluator instructions, and treatment of invalid or unmapped outputs also require clarification. These omissions make the reported accuracy differences difficult to assess.

Important reproducibility details remain missing despite the useful appendices. The allocation of the 15 reported experiments and 33 participants across datasets and conditions is unclear. The exact SBERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, prompt-selection sample sizes, realized codebooks, and per-session outputs are not supplied. Appendix E reports five runs with COVID-sized coverage counts without corresponding Climate details. Code and annotation outputs are promised rather than linked, and the interview analysis procedure is not described sufficiently to reproduce its conclusions.

Several recommendations exceed the demonstrated scope (§§5.4–7). The two corpora differ simultaneously in domain, size, length, and semantic properties, so their comparison cannot identify which characteristics favor a collaboration setting. Similarly, broad conclusions about LLM cost and reliability rest on one 3B model and a particular prompting pipeline, without comparable runtime measurements for the other systems. Narrowing these conclusions, correcting the statistical analysis, and completing the reporting could make a revised submission substantially stronger.
